title: So some food for thought. I went to research and asked when was the last time the Cowboys restructured deals this close to the season and what did they do with it? What we found: This appears to be the first time the Cowboys have restructured multiple deals this close to the season since 2021, when Dak and Ezekiel Elliott's deals were both restructured to clear up a combined ~$12 million in cap space. Jerry at the time said essentially the same thing the team is telling me now it was cap space but always looking around the corner. So what actually happened that year ? No big moves for the Cowboys after that. No trade acquisitions. They ended up rolling over around $4 million in cap into 2022. Now, the number they have freed up in flex is way larger than that, It looks like the Cowboys are now sitting at ~$33 million in cap space after clearing $19 million to go with their $14 million. So let’s hypothetically talk about a player. Raiders and Maxx say he is staying put but if they did move him the team acquiring Crosby would be taking on ~$30.7 million in cap charges from Crosby. OverTheCap explains some options though: “After the trade occurs the acquiring team then has the ability to restructure the contract to bring the salary cap charge down. In Crosby’s case they would convert $28.7 million to a bonus, likely adding a void year in the process, and save $22.96 million in cap room, bringing Crosbys salary cap number for the year down to $7.822 million. However, that does not occur until after the trade. You need the $29.857M to execute the trade not just $7.8 million.” Fascinating stuff. I know nothing. I’ve asked questions. Team sources tell me the money is cap space. We shall see

Jerry at the time said essentially the same thing the team is telling me now it was cap space but always looking around the corner. 

So what actually happened that year ? 

No big moves for the Cowboys after that. No trade acquisitions. They ended up rolling over around $4 million in cap into 2022.

So let’s hypothetically talk about a player.

title: SEC on today’s ruling in Baton Rouge: Statement from the Southeastern Conference on ruling in today’s preliminary hearing: We disagree with the Court’s decision. The SEC’s Presidents and Chancellors unanimously adopted a clear and reasonable standard: member universities should not place former professional athletes on their rosters. The Conference and its member universities have the right to establish, through agreed-upon governance procedures, the rules under which they voluntarily compete and to expect those rules to be followed. The SEC will continue to defend this standard, the principle of fair competition, and the Conference’s authority to govern competition among its member universities.

When I was doing news blurbs for Rotoworld (15+ years ago), we had a rule for training camp: If no info, player had to miss three straight days of camp before we did a blurb.

In today's terminally online era, every time a dude takes a piss it's DEFCON 1.

Not sure if that's good or bad, as we always want as much info as possible. But I do know it's time to start the damn games.

There's life on the other side. And no matter what you're going through, you're loved and people care for you, so hang in there. I know it's tough in this life and Satan tries to grab us at the wrong times, but just know that you are loved and nothing that you're going through other people aren't going through. title: Brian Schottenheimer on Christian Parker’s ability to relate to players: “I think it’s important when you’re communicating in the heat of the moment, the relationships matter. There are a lot of times where you are making a correction, and if you don’t have the relationship, if you don’t have the buy-in from the players at times, players, coaches as well, can tune you out. I don’t think there’s any chance of that happening, because he’s built up a rapport with these guys. “Walked by his office this morning, not surprised, Caleb Downs sitting in there. Door closed, watching film. If you don’t have that, I think it hurts your ability to critique, coach, coach hard, call out. Those are all things we do. If guys make a mistake, we call them out. That’s part of our job description. They need to know you love them and care about them. So, if you don’t spend the time doing that, you’re missing an opportunity.” “… I think (his youth) does help. I didn’t go to three nights straight of Jay Z in New York City. He did. Four or five of our players were there. … I do think that the age does help. They are into the same things. He’s got some really expensive shoes. He’s got some really expensive watches. And so do our players. … That’s real. That’s real that you can relate to your guys like that.”

title: Cowboys QB Dak Prescott on where he’s trying to improve entering Year 11: “Every part of the game. I just think the more that you play, sometimes it gets easier to see things coming. But that doesn’t allow me to know exactly what’s about to happen. So really just staying in the moment, staying where my feet are, not trying to hit a home run each and every play. But just playing the play individually, understanding that every decision I make has an effect on the whole team. So it’s not just one area. As I’ve said, last year was a good year, but I want to be better than that. So, it’s each and every way that I can.”

title: Asked former Orioles catcher Adley Rutschman if he holds any resentment toward Mike Elias, and how would he describe their relationship? Adley: “[Elias] has got a tough job, and he's got to make tough decisions, and I think I always respect that. He’s really good at what he does, and he has reasons for everything that he does, and I've always had a good relationship with him. So it’s just one of those things in baseball that you kind of understand as part of the business aspect of it, and he's got to do what he thinks is best for you know the organization, short term and long term. “I don't have any ill feelings towards anyone in the Orioles organization at all. It’s been nothing but positive, and will continue to be that way.”

title: Here's some more context around Michael Wilson's extension: - As of Wednesday morning, the two sides were about $3 million-$4 million apart, a source told ESPN. The gap was closed quickly and by 3 p.m. Arizona time, Wilson's team was "very optimistic" that a deal would get done. - It was his choice to get three years instead of four. - Wilson's $25 million per year is about $10 million more per year than Arizona's initial offer. - Whenever Wilson's team countered an offer, the Cardinals responded with small, incremental offers. - I didn't see the negotiations going into the season. I was told that Week 1 was a deadline of sorts. - As of late in training camp, I got the sense that a deal was not getting done.

- Wilson's $25 million per year is about $10 million more per year than Arizona's initial offer.
